title: Puffins: Clowns of the Sea
paragraphs: Have you ever seen a bird with a beak as bright as a rainbow? You might spot one on Britain’s cliffs in spring or summer. It is a puffin, a small seabird with a black back, a white front and orange feet. Because of its colourful beak and its waddling walk, the puffin is sometimes called the “clown of the sea”.

An adult puffin is about as long as a 30-centimetre ruler. Puffins spend most of their lives at sea. In autumn and winter, they live far out on the ocean, bobbing on the waves even in wild storms. They only return to land in spring, to raise a family.

Puffins are excellent swimmers. They dive to catch small fish such as sand eels. Underwater, they flap their wings as if they were flying and steer with their webbed feet. A puffin can carry several fish in its beak at once, holding each one in place with its tongue while it catches the next.

Each spring, puffins return to the same cliff tops, often to the very same burrow. A burrow is a tunnel in the ground. Puffins dig burrows with their beaks and feet, or move into old rabbit holes. Deep inside the burrow, the female lays a single egg. Both parents take turns to keep the egg warm for about six weeks.

When the egg hatches, out comes a fluffy black chick called a puffling. Its parents fly back and forth to the sea many times a day, bringing it beakfuls of fish. Safe in the dark burrow, the hungry puffling eats and eats until it grows plump.

Puffins have enemies, too. Large gulls wait on the cliff tops, ready to snatch young birds or steal fish from tired parents. At about six weeks old, the puffling is ready to leave. It waits until dark, then scurries to the cliff edge and flutters down to the sea alone. It will not come back to land for two or three years.

Sadly, puffins are at risk. In some areas, there are fewer sand eels for them to eat, and on some islands, rats eat their eggs and chicks. People are working hard to help. On Lundy, an island off the coast of Devon, rats were removed, and puffins now raise chicks there again.

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 1.
Find and copy one word that means walking with short steps while rocking from side to side.

Look at paragraph 1.
The writer says the puffin has “a beak as bright as a rainbow”.
What does this tell you about the puffin’s beak? Tick one.
options: It is curved like a rainbow.
It is very colourful.
It only appears after rain.
It is extremely large.

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 2.
Puffins bob on the waves “even in wild storms”.
What does this suggest about puffins? Tick one.
options: They are tough birds.
They are afraid of the sea.
They prefer storms to calm weather.
They cannot fly.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 3, what kind of small fish do puffins catch?
Using information from the text, decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: Puffins use their wings to swim underwater.
Puffins steer with their tails when they swim.
Puffins dig their burrows with their beaks and feet.
A puffin can only carry one fish in its beak at a time.

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 5.
…the hungry puffling eats and eats until it grows **plump**.
Which word is closest in meaning to **plump**? Tick one.
options: fluffy
brave
chubby
noisy

questions.prompt: Using the text, explain how a puffin’s life in autumn and winter is different from its life in spring and summer.
questions.model: In autumn and winter, puffins live far out on the ocean, bobbing on the waves even in wild storms. In spring and summer, they come back to land, often to the very same cliff tops, to raise a family in a burrow.
points: what puffins do in autumn and winter (1 mark), e.g. they live far out on the ocean; they bob on the waves, even in wild storms.
what puffins do in spring and summer (1 mark), e.g. they return to land or to the cliff tops; they raise a family in a burrow; they lay an egg and feed their chick.

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 6.
Why do you think the puffling waits until dark before it leaves? Explain, using evidence from the text.
questions.model: I think the puffling waits until dark so that its enemies cannot see it. The text says that “large gulls wait on the cliff tops, ready to snatch young birds”, so if the puffling left in daylight, a gull might catch it before it reached the sea.
points: Explains that in the dark it is harder for enemies to see or catch the puffling
Uses evidence: large gulls wait on the cliff tops, ready to snatch young birds

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 6.
Find and copy **one** word that shows the puffling moves quickly, with small steps.

Look at paragraph 7.
What do you think will happen to the puffins on Lundy in the future?
Use evidence from the text to support your prediction.
questions.model: I think there will be more and more puffins on Lundy, because the rats that ate their eggs and chicks have been removed, and puffins “now raise chicks there again”.
points: a sensible prediction (1 mark), e.g. there will be more puffins on Lundy; more chicks will survive; puffins will keep coming back to nest there.
evidence from the text that supports the prediction (1 mark), e.g. the rats that ate their eggs and chicks were removed; puffins now raise chicks there again; people are working hard to help.
A prediction that numbers might not grow much can also score if it uses evidence, e.g. there are fewer sand eels for them to eat in some areas.

questions.prompt: Number these events from 1 to 5 to show the order in which they happen in a puffin’s year.
items: The puffling flutters down to the sea.
Puffins return to the cliff tops.
Both parents take turns to keep the egg warm.
The female lays a single egg.
The parents bring fish to the puffling.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer begin the text with a question? Tick one.
options: to show that the writer does not know much about puffins
to give the reader instructions
to tell the reader how the text will end
to make the reader curious and want to read on

questions.prompt: Which of these is the best summary of the whole text? Tick one.
options: Puffins are funny birds that perform tricks like clowns.
Puffins are colourful seabirds that spend most of the year at sea, come to land to raise their chicks and are now being helped by people.
Gulls and rats are the biggest dangers to all the birds in Britain.
Puffins spend the whole year in burrows on the cliff tops.
